rewritten_text:
The stars were still shining brightly when I woke, and Taurus, high in the southern sky, told me it was midnight. My sleep had been troubled by dreams. I dreamed I had been invited to Timon’s last feast. I arrived hungry, but when the dishes were uncovered, only hot water rose in clouds of steam that offered no satisfaction. I ran from the angry host, who took Raymond’s form. In my fevered imagination, the vessels he threw after me were filled with foul vapour, and my friend’s body twisted into a thousand shapes before growing into an enormous ghost, its forehead marked by plague. The spreading shadow climbed higher and higher, filling the unbreakable dome that arched over the world, holding it together and enclosing it, and then seeming to struggle to burst through. The nightmare became unbearable. With a great effort I shook off sleep and brought my mind back to reason. My first thought was of Perdita. I must return to her and support her, finding in despair whatever comfort might sustain her wounded heart. I must draw her back from the wild extremes of grief through the strict demands of duty and the gentle tenderness of sorrow.

The stars were my only guide. I turned away from the terrible ruins of the Golden City and, after much effort, managed to make my way outside its walls. There I met a company of soldiers. I borrowed a horse from one of them and hurried to my sister. Even in that short time, the plain had changed. The camp had been taken down, and what remained of the scattered army gathered here and there in small groups. Every face was troubled; every movement showed shock and fear.

With a heavy heart I entered the palace and stood there, afraid to move forward, to speak, or even to look. Perdita sat in the middle of the hall on the marble floor, her head bent against her chest, her hair in disorder, her fingers twisting constantly together. She was as pale as the marble, and pain tightened every feature. She noticed me and looked up in question. The faint hope in her glance was agony. The words died before I could speak them, and I felt a dreadful smile twist my lips. She understood my expression. Her head dropped again, and her fingers resumed their restless movement. At last I found my voice, but its sound frightened her. The unhappy girl had understood my look, and nothing could make her want that terrible news put into firm, unchangeable words. Indeed, she seemed to want to turn my thoughts away from it. Rising from the floor, she whispered, ‘Hush! After so much crying, Clara is asleep. We must not wake her.’

When I stopped weeping, reason and memory returned, and I began to consider more calmly what had happened and how I ought to act. Only a few hours had passed, yet my circumstances had been utterly transformed. Since morning I had lived through changes that should have taken years. My father was dead to me, and for a moment I felt as though he lay white-haired in his coffin while I, my youth lost to advancing age, mourned a death that had come in its proper season. But that was not the truth. I was still young—oh, far too young—and he was not dead to everyone else. Yet I, in my misery, must never see him or speak to him again. I must flee him more urgently than I would my greatest enemy. Whether alone or in a city, I must never again look upon him. The thought left me breathless with anguish, and seized my imagination so completely that for a time I could pursue no other train of thought. From this day forward, I thought, I would live in the bleakest seclusion. I would go to the Continent and become a nun, not out of religious devotion, since I was not a Catholic, but to shut myself away from the world forever. There I would find solitude in which to weep, where the voices of the living could never reach me.

But my father—my beloved, deeply unhappy father? Would he die? Would he never master the fierce passion that now ruled him without pity? Many, many years from now, when age had extinguished the burning feelings that tormented him, might he become my father again? This thought eased the tension in my brow, and I felt—and wept to feel—a faint, sorrowful smile soften the suffering on my lips. I dared to imagine a better future. Years must pass, but hope would give them wings; and even if they passed slowly, they would still pass, and I had not lost my father forever. Let him endure another sixteen years of lonely wandering. Let him once again pour out his wild complaints to vast forests and thunderous waterfalls in a distant land. Let him again face terrifying dangers and hardships that crush the soul. Let the hot southern sun once more burn his passion-worn cheeks, and the cold night rain fall upon him and chill his blood.

To this life, unhappy father, I condemn you! Go! Spend your days among savage peoples and your nights beneath the open sky! Let your limbs grow weary and your heart grow cold, until every trace of youth within you is dead!

I would counterfeit my death; my satisfied heirs would take possession of my riches, and I should buy my liberty. Yet the scheme required cunning; I could not leave myself penniless, and must set aside some money. Alas, what hateful expedients I was forced to adopt! Otherwise, however, a lifetime of deceit awaited me; and whenever remorse at devising a fraud made me recoil from my purpose, the arrival of some aunt or cousin drew me irresistibly back and strengthened my resolve. They would remind me that death was the common fate of mankind, then suggest that my father had certainly been out of his senses since my mother died; that he was mad, and I fortunate, since in one of his fits he might have murdered me rather than put an end to his own distracted existence. All this, of course, was conveyed with delicacy, never in plain terms lest my feelings suffer, but

Murmured thus and so In veiled suggestion, hushed and low

with lowered eyes and compassionate smiles or little cries; and I heard them with a composed face while every nerve shook, I who dared neither assent nor deny such blasphemy. Oh, what a delightful existence, altogether free of deceit! Mine was the face of a dove and the heart of a fox: for I knew only the humiliation of falsehood, with no holy sense of inward innocence to redeem it. I, who once had dressed myself in sincerity’s shining robe, must now borrow a garment of many colours. At first it might hang clumsily upon me, but practice would teach me to arrange its folds gracefully, to tell my lies with elegance. Yes, I might stain my soul with deceit until its original colour was entirely concealed. Oh, dearest father! Receive your unhappy daughter’s pure heart; allow me to come to you as unstained as before, or you will fail to know my transformed appearance. As sorrow might alter Constance, deception would alter me, until in heaven you would declare, ‘This is not my child.’ Father, if I am to be happy now and when we meet once more, I must escape this whole existence, which is a mockery to such a one as I. Only in solitude shall I remain myself; in solitude I shall belong to you.

Alas, even now I remember with disgust the devices and deceptions through which, after many distressing struggles, I accomplished my withdrawal. I could give a lengthy account of the measures I took, first to obtain a small provision for the rest of my days, and then to make my death seem certain. I could do so, but I will not.
